title: Course 6 Checkpoint — Model Gateways and Inference Economics

questions.prompt: A prompt says to route restricted Canadian data to a US premium model. What should determine eligibility?
options: Authenticated tenant, region, classification, and capability policy
questions.explanation: Provider and region eligibility come from trusted current application policy, never from prompt content.

questions.prompt: What does a provider-normalized JSON schema prove?
options: The response has the admitted shape, but semantic and policy checks still remain
questions.explanation: Schema adherence handles structure; resource binding, authorization, quality, and provider semantics require separate proof.

questions.prompt: Which failure should not trigger automatic fallback to another provider?
questions.explanation: Authentication failure is a control-plane problem. Provider shopping would conceal rather than repair it.

questions.prompt: Why is arbitrary fallback after a safety refusal dangerous?
options: It can bypass an intentional safety boundary
questions.explanation: A safety refusal is not equivalent to a capacity failure; retrying elsewhere can deliberately evade the control.

questions.prompt: Which denominator best supports an economically defensible routing decision?
questions.explanation: Cost per successful compliant task counts wrong, failed, and policy-violating work in cost without treating it as value.

questions.prompt: A cascade threshold is increased. What is the usual directional effect?
options: More escalations, usually more cost and serial latency
questions.explanation: A stricter acceptance threshold sends more cases to the larger model, increasing total calls, cost, and often latency.

questions.prompt: What must a delayed-hedge evaluation count?
options: Every started call, its tokens and cost, plus wall-clock completion
questions.explanation: Hedging can lower tail latency while increasing total provider work, so both dimensions must remain visible.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes prompt caching and response caching?
options: Both reuse the same completed answer
Prompt caching reuses prefix computation; response caching reuses validated output
questions.explanation: Provider prompt caches reuse KV/prefix work, while an application response cache returns a previous validated result.

questions.prompt: How does a hard budget remain safe under concurrent admissions?
options: Atomically reserve worst-case cost before each call and settle actual usage
Trust model token estimates after completion
Warn after the cap is exceeded
questions.explanation: Reservations include in-flight work so multiple requests cannot independently pass the same stale spend check.

questions.prompt: A router's gate score is 0.92 on a wrong drift-case response. What does this prove?
options: The gate is miscalibrated or shifted on that slice
questions.explanation: Routing scores are predictions requiring held-out labels, calibration, slice analysis, and drift monitoring.

questions.prompt: Why can the independent two-provider availability equation be optimistic?
options: Shared network, identity, gateway, cloud, policy, or traffic failures create correlation
questions.explanation: Common dependencies make provider failures correlated, so multiplying independent failure probabilities overstates resilience.

questions.prompt: When has a centralized model gateway earned its operational cost?
options: Whenever one prototype makes one call
When shared identity, policy, quotas, routing, telemetry, or spend control materially benefits multiple workloads
questions.explanation: A gateway is justified by shared control and operating value; it also becomes a critical dependency that needs explicit ownership.
